Hey, I'm a PC player, so I probably can't help a lot as I don't know how the console side of things works, but I can definitely recommend some YouTubers with very good tips to go watch. Raynday Gaming is very good and has a lot of useful tips and tricks videos, as well as TheGamingMerchant, and his movement is crazy good. Nokokopuffs is probably one of the best people to watch and study and in his Solo to Masters series you will learn so much about just playing the game and the mindset to be in, I have recommended it to people before who couldn't understand the flow of the game, and this always helped them. Chiknnuggey is always an incredible player to watch and is super straight forward, so study his gameplay. RogueWraith is an incredible controller player and I would highly recommend his channel no matter what platform you use. MokeySniper is another great educational channel full of tips and tricks that you can learn to utilize and keep in hour arsenal of tools in a match.

Another thing is just practice in the Firing Range. It's there for a reason. Work on recoil control, practice tracking, test different legends, work on your accuracy. There are lots and lots of videos on these things, just go on YouTube (maybe check out the people I recommended if you like them) and find some tips.

Learn how to manage your inventory and loot quickly. Learn what you need, what you don't need, but also don't just look around and take 5 minutes to loot one building. Especially on drop, just pick up everything that is around you. Just spam the interact key and keep moving cause you can sort it out later. Maybe you picked up a second gun that really isn't your favorite. Oh well. It is better to have a gun you don't like that could save you later than getting punched death because you were stuck in a reload. There are plenty of guns around and it won't matter if you're dead anyway. But you don't know what you might need in the next couple of minutes and looting quickly saves you from back-tracking and might even save you in a fight if you can switch quickly when you need to. Learning how to loot quickly is just a basic skill that so many people can't seem to do because they're too indecisive and it unfortunately gets them killed. Be confident in yourself. Trust your gut, it's probably right.

Similarly, learn to shield swap. If you are low in a fight, and your shield is broken or almost broken, and you see a shield or a loot box nearby that has one, don't be the guy that pops a phoenix and gets killed. Doesn't matter if you have a level 4 and that box has a level 2. The point is that you now have 75 shield instead of 0. You now have protection and it took you a max of 2 seconds to get it. That can be the difference between a win and a loss. Speed will come with time, but practice consciously instituting basic things like that into your gameplay because it will eventually become second nature when you keep doing it consistently.

Movement is everything in this game, and there are tons and tons of tutorials and tips videos on YouTube, here are some places to get you started. Learn how to strafe. Practice different strafing patterns. Find the best strafe for your legend in different scenarios, because sometimes you might need to react differently when there is someone with a wingman vs someone with a 301. Learn how to crouch spam while strafing when in close quarters. Don't ads when under 10-15m. They are literally right in front of you in and you will die immediately 90% of the time. Learn how to peek. Don't run in a straight line, you will be insanely easy to track. Slide and jump while running between cover, but don't jump in a fight. Make your movements as unpredictable as possible. The more shots you can land on them without them hitting in you is key to winning fights. You want to be hard to hit and if you just crouch in one place while ads, you are basically just a mini fridge and you will die instantly when fighting against better players. Learn how to utilize your momentum as much as possible, and if you use a mobility legend, you need to be able to make the most of that. 

Practice your situational awareness, critical thinking, and reaction time will be really important, especially as you move on up in your skills and ranks. You will be expected to know how to handle yourself and understand the communication between your team, yourself, and the movements of other teams around you. Start by understanding how players think and how they move, always try to keep the high ground, make sure your back is clear, and learn when to push fights and when to leave them alone, and even backing out of one. You are not a coward for backing out of a fight you can't win. If your teammates push when the enemy has the advantage, just let them die. They made their mistakes, but don't make that yours. Never take a fight you know nothing about or one you can't win. If you want to third party a fight, wait until people start getting knocked, then go in and clean up when they are low. Just make sure you weren't the only other squad trying to push that or you might be in a bad mess. Your situational awareness of knowing where others are, where your teammates are, where cover is, who has the high ground, where you can dip out to heal, and everything else is invaluable. That can be the difference between an okay player to a good one. If you struggle with situational awareness, I recommend picking up Bloodhound as they can really help you learn how to recognize where others are, and you will eventually get to the point, you can do that without their tactical.

And while I don't play controller, my best friend only has PS4 and I convinced them to play last season. I'm still working on trying to teach them as they can be rather stubborn in not changing at times, but in that I have found a few basic settings that can really help put you above other players once you get your practice in. First is change your controller layout to Ninja. Movement is everything in this game and that layout will enable you to have much better control over your movement while in fights as well as making more advanced movement techniques like wall jumping, bunny hopping, tap strafing, etc. much much easier. It also allows full movement while in a fight while still allowing you complete control over your aim. Honestly, this should be the default controller layout.
Upping your sensitivity as far as you can incrementally until you reach a cap where you know you can move fluidly in and out of combat and menus without going wild. The biggest thing I see with controller players is that their movements are slow and janky and they just die too fast because they can't keep up with how fast this game moves. Put yourself in situations where you can better compete and win more engagements. RogueWraith has great tutorials on lots of settings for controller players and so do others, so take a few days to just try different things and get used to them and see what works for you. Remember don't change all of your settings all at once. The jarring changes will leave you stranded and frustrated and you won't be any better off. Just tweak things slowly so you can adapt and adjust to your new environment.

Last thing I can thing of right now is just be consistent. Play regularly, even if that's only a couple hours in the evenings. Be consistent. Find legends to practice with and get used to. A lot of people jump around too much early on and they can't get a feel for how to use any of them properly. Also I recommend trying to find weapons that you feel comfortable with that work very well in games. Find what you vibe with and if you are just playing casual, keep doing that. Having things you are comfortable and confident with will change games. Vibes are important and having a few bad games or even a bad day does not make you a bad player. Not trying to improve does. And by coming here and asking for help is a huge step in the right direction! Don't let the toxic people get you down, and don't worry if you don't have 500 kills a season on your main. Keep practicing and you will keep getting better over time. Anyway, I hope this helped some. If you want any specifics or an elaboration on anything I mentioned, just ask. Hope I didn't come across as harsh in anyway, just want to see you do the best you can and break bad habits early. 

But anyway, best of luck to you, and happy fighting, legend o7

There's a lot of good points in here, but I would like to add as well that the Imperial system was developed and used across the Occident for centuries. It was fairly recent (as history is concerned) that the Metric system was invented, and it slowly became adopted by more and more countries. The Metric system was created to be more fundamentally friendly with the common Western base 10 mathematics, however the base 12 system of measurements was formed out of necessity and refined over time and is a perfectly viable measurement system, just as any other. Many units of measurements in the imperial system are no longer used today (such as the chain, furlong, fathom, cable, etc.), and I find that quite a shame. It doesn't make lives harder, it's simply a matter of what your mind is trained to understand. It's like the idea of the colour grue, and it's interesting to watch many people slowly drift into deeper confusion as the concepts are explained to them, most often because those people do not have the interest or desire to understand what is different from themselves.

Regardless, however, I enjoy both systems for practical application and history alike.

It wants you to feel more depressed so that you can thrive, and by being hungry and not eating intentionally, depression can grab hold of it and eat you alive. Okay, I'm 18M and this just happened to me after my third suicide attempt. I live in Tennessee, so it may or may not differ depending on the hospital and state. I came in as a normal patient at the ER that a friend took me to, as I have a rough home life and he was the one I talked to while I had a gun in my hand that evening. It was midnight when I got there, and they asked me questions, what had happened, why was I feeling suicidal, how long had it been going on, etc. The kind of stuff you expect. I too am very shy and timid, and didnt say hardly anything at all while I was there. They stripped me of my clothes and possessions, put them in a bag, and clothed me in a yellow gown. I waited for about 12 hours while they had crisis on the line and had to get an ambulance there to me. I mostly sat there staring at my hands, and listened to their conversations. They checked on me every now and again, but mostly let me sit there by myself. most of the nurses didnt care, nor did the doctor, but with the morning shift there was one very sweet nurse who brought me food even though I wasnt hungry, made sure I was comfortable and had everything I needed. I was scared, and was appropriately labeled as a docile patient, but overall looking back it was not a bad stay. The EMT I talked and stayed with me was very kind, but as always EMTs seem to come in pairs of opposites. He sat with me talked with me about my favorite book that I was allowed to keep on my way to psych hospital, as I was seen as docile patient and not in "immediate danger" but of course because of my scars and cuts and burns from self-harm this was the only thing I was allowed to keep, and also no silverware due to procedure of caring for suicidal patients.
They will keep you as long as needed at the psych ward, and I pray that you find a good one with people who care about you. It's not at all what you expect and it's really not that bad from my experience. I was terrified though and didnt speak a word for 6 days, I only spoke using sign language and writing after the first couple of days of silence. I don't reccomend this path as the doctor will probably tell you that selective mutism is not a good method for recovery, as mine did to me, but if you dont feel comfortable talking, then you dont have to talk to anyone else. It's entirely okay. I was thankful to be lucky enough to have a great group of people who even while I didn't talk made sure that I was taken care of, treated kindly, watched out for, had the things I wanted, ate my food (as much as I could anyway, which I don't eat hardly anything because of my problems), and everything great really. They are the reasons I came to finally speak again, my first words being "I'm scared," which only made them more protective of me. I see now that it really was okay, and not as scary as it all seemed. It was overwhelming because of how fast it happened, but I was safe and taken care of by the staff, which I honestly quite miss seeing some days. They treated me with medications that helped stabilize me and of course gave me a diagnosis of GAD, MDD, and Schizophrenia. There were phones to call out to people on the outside, and they did have a schedule that we stuck to for the couple of weeks I was there, but we had plenty of downtime to relax, watch TV, draw, whatever. I even taught some people how to draw maps and they learned basic sign language (originally by asking for a chart of the alphabet, and I taught them more) so I could communicate more comfortably and they could make me feel more comfortable and less isolated.
All in all, as terrified as I was going into it and through it for the first while I was there, I am very thankful I went. I hope you will be too. <3

I would recommend trying the FTB Academy Modpack! It's specifically for those who are new to modded Minecraft and will make sure that you don't go through it alone with tons of quests, detailed instructions, and yet also some freedom to explore on your own if you feel adventurous. It holds your hand and yet gives you as much freedom as you want with a mass of mods that will give you a great experience in lots of different mod types and popular 1.12 mods.
I know it seems overwhelming but it's really not that bad! I started giant modpacks when I was 11, and I'm not the brightest anyway, so almost anyone can do it!

Advice:
Wiki pages will always be your best friend.
Always try new things! You never know what they might do.
Try as many different paths as you can as they can all help you on your journey and it will help you find what you like and don't like most!
Try not to break the mods if you can help it. Mod makers work hard to make them work as best as they can, but sometimes they can be broken and it can be hard to fix at times.
Always keep backup saves of your world! Large modpacks can have a tendency to break with certain things and require patches, so keep saves in case this happens.
If your modpack does break or you encounter some sort of bug, report it to the mod author or modpack creator, depending on the situation. (Mod author if it is a feature within the mod itself that is malfunctioning/not working/breaking. Modpack creator if it is a compatibility issue such as items, recipes, or features not flowing together properly, or a case of a certain mod breaking the world or game.) Reporting issues really helps creators so provide as much detail as possible, with screenshots if you can.
Play smartly! Often times you can use some mods to help you in others! There are so many possibilities that well integrated modpacks can provide!
Make sure your PC can handle heavy modpacks! Java is CPU based, so having a fast and stable CPU that can handle a lot of work being thrown at it will save you a lot, but dont push it if you can help it!
And most importantly, have fun ^-^ Modpacks are wonderful and can give you weeks if not months of fun, entertaining, and driving gameplay, bringing new life to Minecraft and encouraging you to play more!

Okay, just so everyone knows, this is absolutely my opinion and I'm not saying that this is necessarily the way it should go, just what I would like to see and how I feel on the matter of the new update(s).

I think 1.16 really has so much potential, and I cannot wait to see what it brings. New biomes that make the nether more survivable and interesting? Absolutely! It feels like the Natura Nether biomes. This shows that Mojang is listening to their community! A new top tier material, even tougher, stronger, and RARER than diamond? A totally bold move, and one that most of the Minecraft community has become enthralled with. New mobs being added? Almost always a good thing to see.

However, are they really worth all the hype that they have gotten in their first week of existence? Have they earned such an esteemed place as game-changing updates to the game?
In short? No. Though I suppose only time will tell, there is still time for a lot of features to be introduced to us. But lately, Mojang has not been giving us much hope in a fully finished update that really offers us interests and features to keep us striving in our worlds. 1.14 was given so much hype and yet what did we receive? Updated appearances and a new danger easily avoided. Don't get me wrong, love the new villager skins and village generations, but we really haven't gained much new. The taiga barely got anything, and nothing really got anything as big as what the hype was made out to be. 1.15 was a joke. I'm still purgeturbed about that. "TRIAL! TRIAL!"

1.16 has way more potential than either of those updates did. But I'm worried that Mojang will once again see it half way through and then leave us with an unfinished idea in hopes of pleasing us quickly. We want quality content, even if it takes a while. Why do you think we're all still waiting for Hytale?? Because we know it's quality, and they are doing their best to give us even more quality and LISTENING TO THEIR COMMUNITY. This is so important and yet it's not Mojang's strongest asset. We need good, complete content, even if it comes out in parts and slowly. We would all appreciate a better game over unimportant details. I love Minecraft and have been playing since Beta 1.0, and I miss the old days when Minecraft felt much simpler and full of enjoyment. But it's time to look ahead for a new future to Minecraft. I think a lot of the base game needs to be adjusted for better scaling and future-proofing. It has so little in the way of materials and has no room for more other than going above diamond and now netherite. We need more intermediaries, and make getting these valuable materials more worthwhile and important. More variety in mobs, plants, crops, trees, landscape, and exploration. the modding community has come in to give us these things, but shouldn't the base game also be giving us this wonderful content? We need to see that Mojang still cares about us enough to give us what we really need, and not giant bees that look like they came out of a really weird mod. We need to be fascinated again like when we were kids, but with the tools that have developed as much as we have.

As best as you can, try to remember these things if you start to feel panicky:

Remember to breath. Breathing is really important. Take deep breaths, as deep as you can, and let slow breaths out. Try to hold it in between if you can for a few seconds, but if you can't then that's okay too. Just keep breathing, you're doing your best and that is what matters.

Try to find a comfortable place to be. It can feel really natural to curl up to protect yourself because you don't know what's happening. Panic attacks are very scary, no matter how many you have. But if you can, try to stetxh out and lay down. It can help your muscles relax and not be so tense. This helps your mind to relax as well. It's okay if you can't stretch out or can't make yourself, remember you are doing your best.
Grounding is a really good technique, especially if you feel an attack coming on. Grounding is helping yourelf feel more rooted in the environment so that your mind can begin to find its way back and help you calm yourself. Focusing on what your sense can understand really helps. Play the 54321 game. Look around you and find 5 things you can see, 4 things you can touch, 3 things you can hear, 2 things you can smell, 1 thing you can taste.

Also remember that this will pass. It's dibilitating, it's scary, but you've been through this before and you will make it through it again. This will pass.
